# Problem 7.1
## a
Simulate 200 realizations from the mixture distribution in 
$\delta N(7, 0.5^2) + (1 - \delta)N(10, 0.5^2)$ with 
$\delta=0.7$. Draw a histogram of these data. \
```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(95)
d0 <- rbinom(200,1,0.7)
sims <- d0*rnorm(200,7,0.5)+(1-d0)*rnorm(200,10,0.5)
hist(sims, main="N(7,0.25) and N(10,0.25) Mixture")
```

## b
Implement an independence chain MCMC procedure to simulate from the posterior
distribution of $\delta$, using your data from part (a). \
```{r,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
n <- 100000
x_vals1 <- NULL
keep <- 1001:n # i.e. first 1000 values are the burn-in

dist <- function(delta) {prod(delta*dnorm(sims,mean=7,sd=0.5) + 
                               (1-delta)*dnorm(sims,mean=10,sd=0.5))} # likelihood
proposal <- function(x) dbeta(x,10,5) # proposal density
ratio <- function(xt,x){dist(x)*proposal(xt)/(dist(xt)*proposal(x))} # ratio, MH algorithm

set.seed(95)
x_vals1[1] <- rbeta(1,10,5)
indy_chain_start <- Sys.time()
for(i in 1:n){
      xt <- x_vals1[i]
      x <- rbeta(1,10,5) # generate from proposal
      prob <- min(ratio(xt,x),1) # compute acceptance probability 
      move <- rbinom(1,1,prob) # move or not move w.p. p
      x_vals1[i+1] <- x*move + xt*(1-move) # move is 0 or 1, so next value is x or xt
}
indy_chain <- Sys.time() - indy_chain_start
rm(indy_chain_start,xt,x,prob,move,i)
x_vals1 <- x_vals1[keep]
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(x_vals1,main=c("Sample Mean:",mean(x_vals1) %>% round(4)))
plot(x_vals1,ylim=c(0,1),type="l",ylab="delta",xlab="t",main="Exploration Plot")
```

## c
Implement a random walk chain with 
$\delta^* = \delta^{(t)} + \epsilon,  \epsilon \sim Unif(-1,1)$ \
```{r,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
set.seed(95)
log_like <- function(delta) {
  sum(log(delta*dnorm(sims,7,.5)+(1-delta)*dnorm(sims,10,.5)))
  }
i <- 1
rw_start <- Sys.time()
p <- rep(0,n) # initial values
p[1] <- rbeta(1,10,5)
while (i < n) {
  pnew <- p[i] + runif(1,-1,1)
  if (pnew >= 0 & pnew <=1) {
    p[i+1] <- pnew
    R <- exp(log_like(p[i+1]) - log_like(p[i]))
    if (R < 1){ 
	    if(rbinom(1,1,R)==0){p[i+1] <- p[i]} # reset to previous value if binom 0
    }
    i <- i+1 # increment i only if delta is valid 
	}
}
x_vals2 <- p
rand_walk <- Sys.time() - rw_start
rm(rw_start,i,p,R,pnew)
x_vals2 <- x_vals2[keep]
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(x_vals2,main=c("Sample Mean:",mean(x_vals2) %>% round(4)))
plot(x_vals2,ylim=c(0,1),type="l",ylab="delta",xlab="t",main="Exploration Plot")
```

## d
Reparameterize the problem letting $U = log[\delta/(1 - \delta)]$ and $U^* = u(t) + \epsilon$.
Implement a random walk chain in U-space as in 
$$\frac{f(logit^{-1}(u^*))*|J(u^*)|*g(u^{(t)}|u^*)}{f(logit^{-1}(u^{(t)}))*|J(u^{(t)})|*g(u^*|u^{(t)})}$$ \
where $|J(u^*)|=\frac{1}{|J(\delta^*)|}$, and $logit(p)=log(\frac{p}{1-p})$
```{r,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
set.seed(95)
u <- rep(0,n)
u[1] <- runif(1,-1,1)
p <- rep(0,n)
p[1] <- exp(u[1])/(1+exp(u[1]))

log_like <- function(delta,data) {
  sum(log(delta*dnorm(data,7,.5)+(1-delta)*dnorm(data,10,.5)))
  }

uspace_start <- Sys.time()
for (i in 1:(n-1)) {
  u[i+1] <- u[i] + runif(1,-1,1)
	p[i+1] <- exp(u[i+1])/(1+exp(u[i+1]))
	R <- exp(log_like(p[i+1],sims) - log_like(p[i],sims)) * 
	  (p[i+1]*(1-p[i+1]))/(p[i]*(1-p[i])) # Jacobian
	if (R < 1){ # M-H algorithm
	  if(rbinom(1,1,R)==0){ # don't move 
		  p[i+1] <- p[i]
		  u[i+1] <- u[i]
		}
	}
}
x_vals3 <- p

uspace <- Sys.time() - uspace_start
rm(uspace_start,i,u,p,R)
x_vals3 <- x_vals3[keep]
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(x_vals3,main=c("Sample Mean:",mean(x_vals3) %>% round(4)))
plot(x_vals3,ylim=c(0,1),type="l",ylab="delta",xlab="t",main="Exploration Plot")
```

## e
Compare the estimates and convergence behavior of the three algorithms.\
```{r}
run_times <- rbind(indy_chain,rand_walk,uspace)
estimates <- rbind(mean(x_vals1),mean(x_vals2),mean(x_vals3))
data.frame(Time=run_times, Estimate=estimates,Absolute_Error=abs(estimates-0.7))
```
The results can vary from run to run and across different seeds. In this 
run the independence chain was the fastest, u-space the slowest, while random
walk was the closest to the true value of $\delta$, independence chain the 
furthest. The reason u-space takes slightly longer is probably due to there
being more lines of code involved in the algorithm. In any case, all results are
extremely comparable, and the paths all show good mixing.

# Problem 7.2
## a
Implement a Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to simulate from 
$\delta N(7, 0.5^2) + (1 - \delta)N(10, 0.5^2)$ with $\delta = 0.7$, using 
$N(x^{(t)}, 0.01^2)$ as the proposal distribution. For each of three starting 
values, $x^{(0)} = 0, 7, 15$, run the chain for 10,000 iterations. Plot the 
sample path of the output from each chain. If only one of the sample paths was 
available, what would you conclude about the chain? For each of the simulations, 
create a histogram of the realizations with the true density superimposed on the 
histogram. Based on your output from all three chains, what can you say about 
the behavior of the chain? \
```{r,warning=FALSE,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
set.seed(95)
mh_algo <- function(ini_mu,n=10000,burn=1000,delt=0.7,stdev=0.01){
  # target function, proposal (iteratively updates), ratio for M-H algorithm
  density <- function(x) delt*dnorm(x,mean=7,sd=0.5) + (1-delt)*dnorm(x,mean=10,sd=0.5)
  proposal <- function(x,mu) dnorm(x,mu,sd=stdev)
  ratio <- function(xt,x_star) density(x_star)*proposal(xt,mu=xt)/
    (density(xt)*proposal(x_star,mu=xt))
  
  x_vals <- NULL
  x_vals[1] <- rnorm(1,ini_mu,stdev) # initial value
  for(i in 1:n){
    xt <- x_vals[i] # proposed next value
    x_star <- rnorm(1,xt,stdev) # generate from proposal with current mean
    
    # print(ratio(xt,x_star))
    prob <- min(ratio(xt,x_star),1)
    move <- rbinom(1,1,prob) # move or not move w.p. prob
    # this is almost always moving, ratio is either close to 1 or greater than 1
    x_vals[i+1] <- x_star*move + xt*(1-move) # move is 0 or 1, next value is xt or x
  }
  keep <- (burn+1):n
  x_vals <- x_vals[keep]
  
  # for overlaying true density
  d <- rbinom(n-burn,1,prob=delt)
  true_vals <- d*rnorm(n-burn,7,0.5) + (1-d)*rnorm(n-burn,10,0.5)
  all_values <- data.frame(x_vals,true_vals)
  post_draws <- ggplot(all_values) +
                  geom_histogram(aes(x=x_vals,y=..density..),bins=50) +
                  geom_density(aes(x=true_vals),col = "red") +
                  ggtitle("Sampled Values from N(7,0.25) and N(10,0.25) Mixture",
                          paste("Initial Mean:",ini_mu,", n:",n,sep=" "))
  # sample path
  path <- ggplot(data=data.frame(x=x_vals,t=1:(n-burn))) +
            geom_line(mapping=aes(x=t,y=x_vals)) +
            ylim(c(-1,16)) + # kept constant to compare plots
            ggtitle("Exploration Plot",
                    paste("Initial Mean:",ini_mu,sep=" "))
  return(list(Sample_Histogram=post_draws,Exploration_Plot = path))
}
mh_algo(ini_mu=0,n=10000,burn=1000)
mh_algo(ini_mu=7,n=10000,burn=1000)
mh_algo(ini_mu=15,n=10000,burn=1000)
```

If we saw any of the proposals alone, we'd conclude that the algorithm did not
converge and we have not successfully sampled from the distribution. This is 
because the standard deviation of the proposal distribution is very small, 
meaning the algorithm is not exploring much outside its initial area. With much
larger sample sizes, we may eventually expect the algorithm to reach better 
regions, but this would likely require n's *many* magnitudes larger. Initial 
$x^{(t)}$ of 7 appears to be the "best", but it is still a very poor fit. We see
that each super-imposed density plot is a pretty poor fit.

## b
Change the proposal distribution to improve the convergence properties of the
chain. Using the new proposal distribution, repeat part (a). \
```{r,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
# I specified a standard deviation parameter in the function, which allows
# us to test different (normal) proposal distributions
mh_algo(ini_mu=0,n=100000,burn=5000,stdev=1)
mh_algo(ini_mu=7,n=100000,burn=5000,stdev=1)
mh_algo(ini_mu=15,n=100000,burn=5000,stdev=1)
```

Exploration plots suggest the algorithm is rapidly jumping back and forth
between the two modes (7 and 10) of the mixture density. It looks like a 
$N(x^{(t)},1)$ proposal density over-samples the second mode. Increasing the 
proposal standard deviation will eventually fill up around 7 in the true density, 
but dramatically over-sample around 10. In any case, this is significantly better
than the previous results. Interestingly, the plots seem to be extremely similar
regardless of starting value. This is probably because the relatively large
standard deviation allows the algorithm to "escape the bad areas" and get into
the good ones (i.e. where the probability density actually lies)

# Problem 7.5
## a
Data Summary and Plots \
```{r,message=FALSE}
cancer <- read_table("C:/Users/jacma/OneDrive/school work/UMD/Stat 705 Computational Stats/Data/datasets/breastcancer.dat")
cancer$treatment <- factor(cancer$treatment)
cancer$censored <- factor(cancer$censored)
# Division by censoring
table(cancer$censored) # 75.7%  were censored
censored_cancer <- subset(cancer,censored==1)
uncensored_cancer <- subset(cancer,censored==0)

# Division by treatment (via plotting)
table(cancer$treatment) # 51.4% received treatment

## Censored recurrence times (Trt: treatment, Ctrl: control)
ggplot(data=censored_cancer) +
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(x=treatment,y=recurtime,color=treatment)) +
  ylim(c(0,60)) + # keep same axes
  ggtitle("Censored Time for Trt/Ctrl") 

## Uncensored recurrence times
ggplot(data=uncensored_cancer) +
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(x=treatment,y=recurtime,color=treatment)) +
  ylim(c(0,60)) +
  ggtitle("Recurrence Time for Trt/Ctrl")
```

The first plot simply shows the number of months for which a patient was observed
*without* recurrence, meaning the recurrence is known to *exceed* these values. 
The second plot shows that the recurrence time for treatment and control groups 
are largely pretty similar, but the treatment group has a lower median and 
tighter inter-quartile range (albeit a higher maximum). This initially implies 
that treatment *decreases* recurrence times, meaning the treatment is *not* 
effective because the patient has cancer again sooner. **However**, the first 
plot having the treatment group above the non-treatment group may have the 
effect of "pulling" the second box plots upward, perhaps to a point where the 
treatment group lies above the control group. Since we know patients in the
first must have avoided recurrence for at least one more month, it is a matter of
*how much* longer the recurrence was avoided for each respective group among 
censored patients. If the treatment for the censored group leads to much longer 
survival times, it could be that treatment *increases* recurrence times, leading 
to the conclusion that hormone therapy is an effective treatment for cancer.

## b
Derive the conditional distributions necessary to implement the Gibbs sampler.\
![]("C:/Users/jacma/OneDrive/school work/UMD/Stat 705 Computational Stats/HW Images/705 HW10 3b.jpg")

## c
Program and run your Gibbs sampler. Use a suite of convergence diagnostics to
evaluate the convergence and mixing of your sampler. Interpret the diagnostics.\
```{r}
# a function which takes in values for the hyperparameters, initial guesses for
# theta and tau, sample size and number to discard from beginning of algorithm
gibbers <- function(hyper_parameters,theta_tau=c(1,1),n=10000,burn=1000,seed=0,data=cancer){
  set.seed(seed)
  
  ### Data Values
  treatment_group <- subset(data,data$treatment==1)
  Hsum <- sum(treatment_group$censored==0) # non-censored treatment observations
  trt_times <- sum(treatment_group$recurtime)
  ctrl_group <- subset(data,data$treatment==0)
  Csum <- sum(ctrl_group$censored==0) # non-censored treatment observations
  ctrl_times <- sum(ctrl_group$recurtime)
  
  initial <- theta_tau # save initial guess
  a <- hyper_parameters[1] # extract hyper_parameter values
  b <- hyper_parameters[2]
  c <- hyper_parameters[3]
  d <- hyper_parameters[4]
  
  param_history <- matrix(0,nrow=n,ncol=2)
  ### Gibbs Sampler
  for (i in 1:n){
    new_params <- theta_tau
    new_params[1] <- rgamma(1, shape=a+1+Csum+Hsum, 
                            rate=c+ctrl_times+new_params[2]*(d+trt_times)) 
    new_params[2] <- rgamma(1, shape=b+Hsum+1, rate=new_params[1]*(d+trt_times))
    param_history[i,] <- new_params
    theta_tau <- new_params
  }
  param_history <- param_history[-(1:burn),] # remove burn-in values
  
  ### Summary Statistics
  post_means <- colMeans(param_history)
  post_sd <- apply(param_history,2,sd)
  post_low_limit <- apply(param_history,2,quantile,probs=0.025)
  post_high_limit <- apply(param_history,2,quantile,probs=0.975)
  summary_statistics <- data.frame(Parameter=NA,
                                   Mean=post_means,StdDev=post_sd,
                                   Low95=post_low_limit,
                                   High95=post_high_limit)
  summary_statistics$Parameter[1] <- "Theta" # probably a much more elegant way 
  summary_statistics$Parameter[2] <- "Tau"
  
  ### Plotting
  param_history <- data.frame(param_history)
  colnames(param_history) <- c("Theta","Tau")
  theta_plot <- ggplot(data=param_history) +
    geom_line(mapping=aes(x=1:(n-burn),y=Theta))+
    xlab("t") + 
    ggtitle("Posterior of Theta",
            paste("Initial Value:",initial[1],
                  ", Hyperparameters: ",a,b,c,d, sep=" "))
  
  tau_plot <- ggplot(data=param_history) +
    geom_line(mapping=aes(x=1:1:(n-burn),y=Tau))+
    xlab("t") + 
    ggtitle("Posterior of Tau",
            paste("Initial Value:",initial[2],
                  ", Hyperparameters: ",a,b,c,d, sep=" "))
  
  return(list(all_values=param_history,
              theta_path=theta_plot,
              tau_path=tau_plot,
              summary_stats=summary_statistics))
}
result1 <- gibbers(c(3,1,60,120))
result1$theta_path
result1$tau_path
```
The plots seem to show pretty good mixing, as neither get stuck at any 
particular value (i.e. not moving). There also seems to be a somewhat reasonable 
number of outliers (very large values) in either plot. A few of these are 
expected due to the generation of thousands of random numbers.

## e
Create a graph which shows the prior and estimated posterior distribution for 
$\tau$ superimposed on the same scale.\
```{r,out.width="80%",out.height="80%"}
# we should see some kind of shift between the prior and the posterior
trt <- subset(cancer,cancer$treatment==1)
theta_mean <- result1$summary_stats$Mean[1]
prior <- rgamma(9000,shape=1+sum(trt$censored==0)+1,
                rate=theta_mean*(120+sum(trt$recurtime)))

tau_vals <- data.frame(post_value = result1$all_values$Tau,
                       prior_value = prior) 
ggplot(tau_vals) +
  geom_density(aes(x=post_value),col='red') +
  geom_density(aes(x=prior_value),col='blue') +
  ggtitle("Prior of Tau (Blue) vs Posterior of Tau (Red)")
```

The posterior is in red, the prior in blue. We see that the posterior spread out
the mass around 1 more widely than the prior, which is intuitive based on the 
results we obtained. 

## f
Interpret the results. Specifically, what does your estimate of $\tau$ mean for 
the clinical trial? Are the recurrence times for the hormone group significantly 
different from those for the control group? \

$Time_{T}\sim Exp(\tau \theta)$ and $Time_{C}\sim Exp(\theta)$. \
With $\theta$ held constant, $\tau>1$ decreases the expected recurrence time
(since the expected value of an exponential is 1 over its rate parameter 
$\frac{1}{\tau\theta}$, which goes to 0 as $\tau \rightarrow \infty$), meaning 
the treatment is ineffective because patients are returning *more* frequently. 
If we had $\tau<1$, the expected recurrence time would increase, meaning 
patients return *less* frequently, suggesting the treatment is *effective*. 
($\frac{1}{\tau\theta} \rightarrow \infty$ as $\tau \rightarrow 0$).\
$\tau=1$ would mean that there is no difference in recurrence time between the 
treatment and control group. \
To determine whether or not recurrence times are significantly different for the
hormone group compared to the control group, the entire confidence interval of 
alpha would have to be above or below 1. Above 1 can allow us to conclude that
treatment significantly *decreases* recurrence times, while an interval below one 
can allow us to conclude that treatment significantly *increases* recurrence 
times. The situation in which recurrence times *decrease* is the situation that 
implies the treatment did not work, because patients are expected to return with
cancer more frequently. Thus, a confidence interval entirely above 1 suggests
hormonal therapy is significantly *ineffective* and improving recurrence times.

## g
Sensitivity analysis: repeat your Gibbs sampler for values of the hyperparameters 
that are half and double the original hyperparameter values. Provide a table of 
summary statistics to compare your results. Based on your results, what 
recommendations do you have for the drug company regarding the sensitivity of 
your results to hyperparameter values?
```{r}
results2 <- gibbers(c(1.5,0.5,30,60)) # half hyperparameters
results2$summary_stats
results2$tau_path

results3 <- gibbers(c(6,2,120,240)) # double hyperparameter
results3$summary_stats
results3$tau_path
```

Both halving and doubling the hyperparameters seems to have little effect on the
results. All summary statistics for both parameters are very similar, and most
notably, the 95% credible interval for $\tau$ contains 1, suggesting there is
no signficant effect of hormone therapy. The sample paths also look very similar
in shape and in mixing. \
This outcome suggests that the data is robust to the hyperprior - one might say 
that the data "dominates" the hyperprior, since the values of the hyperparameters
have little to no effect on the results once data is seen. It should be noted
that the mean and 95% interval for $\tau$ with the halved hyperparameters are 
greater, but the conclusion would not differ as they all contain 1. \
My recommendation might be to consider different prior and/or model formulations,
since the value of the hyperparameters do not seem to have much of an effect on 
the results. This could alter conclusions in some respect, and may be achieved 
by the inclusion of additional hyperpriors or simply using a different set-up.
One might also consider implementing Metropolis-within-Gibbs in set-ups where
the resulting posterior is difficult to sample from.
